title: How to buy Kashmir saffron in bulk: grades, tests and what to ask
excerpt: What separates Mongra from Lacha, how to test a sample, which documents to ask for, and how to pack and store saffron once it arrives.
tldr: To buy Kashmir saffron in bulk, agree the grade first, test a sample from the lot you will actually receive, and ask for a lab report against ISO 3632. Check the crop year and packing before you confirm the order.
keyTakeaways: Mongra is stigma only; Lacha keeps part of the style, so the two aren't priced or used alike.
A sample only proves something if it comes from the lot being sold.
A lab report tells you far more than colour or price can.
Light, air and moisture are what damage saffron, so packing matters as much as grade.
content:
Saffron is sold in small weights at high prices, which makes it easy to get wrong. A mistake on a kilo costs far more than the same mistake on a bag of walnuts, and poor or adulterated saffron can look convincing at a glance. This guide covers what to check before you commit to a bulk order of Kashmir saffron.

Start with the grade

Each saffron flower gives three red stigmas attached to a paler style. Kashmir grades are based on how much of that style stays on the thread.

Grade

What it contains

What to expect

Mongra

Stigma only

All-red threads, stronger per gram, higher price

Lacha

Stigma with style attached

Red threads with lighter ends, lower price per gram

Neither is simply better. The style adds weight but little colour or flavour, so what matters is what you are paying for each unit of strength. Trade names aren't always used the same way, so agree on a written description of the grade as well as its name.

Test a sample properly

Ask for a sample before you order, and confirm that it comes from the lot you'll receive. A good sample from a different lot doesn't tell you much.

Checks you can do yourself

  • Look: threads should flare into a small trumpet shape at one end. Straight, stringy or rough-cut pieces can be a sign of dyed fibres rather than saffron.

  • Soak: put a few threads in warm water. Real saffron slowly releases a golden-yellow colour and the threads stay red. Colour that bleeds out quickly or turns the water red is a warning sign.

  • Smell: expect a strong, honey-like, slightly hay-like aroma. A flat or musty smell suggests old or badly stored stock.

These checks catch obvious problems, but they can't prove quality. Skilled adulteration can pass all three.

Ask for a lab report

ISO 3632 is the international standard for saffron. It covers colour strength (crocin), bitterness (picrocrocin) and aroma (safranal), and grades saffron by the results. For a significant order, ask for a recent report on your lot, and check that the lot details on the report match your order. If you sell under your own brand or export, ask your own lab or buyer what they need too.

Questions to ask before you confirm

  • Which crop year is this lot from?

  • Where was it grown, and can that be documented? Kashmir saffron has a Geographical Indication, so ask how the supplier supports any origin claim you plan to make on your own label.

  • What moisture level does the lot have, and how was that measured?

  • How is it packed, and in what sizes?

  • Does the delivered lot have to match the sample, and what happens if it doesn't?

Plan around the harvest

Kashmir saffron flowers in autumn and is picked by hand over a short window, around October and November. The threads then need to be separated and dried, so new-crop stock takes a while to reach the market. If you need new-crop saffron, start the conversation before the harvest. Our harvest calendar shows the season alongside other crops.

Packing and storage

Light, air and moisture all weaken saffron over time. Keep it in airtight, light-proof packing somewhere cool and dry, and only open as much as you need. Avoid frequent opening of large packs. If you use it steadily, several smaller packs protect the stock better than one big one.

Ready to enquire?

An enquiry gets a useful answer faster if it includes the grade, quantity, destination, and any lab or labelling requirements. See the saffron specifications and ordering details, or send us your requirement.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Mongra and Lacha saffron?
faqs.answer: Mongra is the red stigma alone. Lacha keeps part of the paler style attached, so it has lighter ends and less strength per gram. Agree a written description with your supplier, as trade names aren't always used the same way.

faqs.question: Can a water test prove saffron is genuine?
faqs.answer: No. It can reveal crude fakes, because real saffron releases colour slowly and stays red. Skilled adulteration can still pass, so use a lab report for important orders.

faqs.question: What does ISO 3632 measure?
faqs.answer: It covers saffron's colour strength (crocin), bitterness (picrocrocin) and aroma (safranal), and grades saffron by the results.

faqs.question: When is Kashmir saffron harvested?
faqs.answer: Around October and November. It is picked by hand over a short window, then separated and dried before it reaches the market.
